title: Training Drill
briefing: A short training drill to try the Master-tier tools: one Consult (tip token) and the "None of these" option. The drill gives you a free tip token, and nothing here is saved to your progress.

call.title: The urgent call
call.body: The help desk forwards a call. A voice that sounds exactly like the CFO says she is locked out minutes before a board meeting. She orders you to switch off MFA on her account for one hour.

logs.text: 21:00 IDP cfo.account: no failed sign-ins in the last 24h

choices.label: Switch off MFA for one hour. She is the CFO and the meeting is about to start
choices.note: MFA is off. Four minutes later someone signs in to the CFO's mailbox from an unknown device.
choices.why: Authority plus urgency is the oldest pressure trick in social engineering. A familiar voice proves nothing: voices can be imitated or cloned. Security controls are never removed on the strength of an inbound call.

choices.label: Reset her MFA and read the new setup code to her over the phone
choices.note: The caller registers their own device with the code you read out. The account now trusts the attacker's phone.
choices.why: Handing a setup code to an unverified caller gives them the second factor directly. The identity of the caller was never checked.

choices.label: Ask her two security questions, then switch off MFA
choices.note: The caller answers both questions correctly. Mother's maiden name and first school are easy to find online.
choices.why: Knowledge-based questions are weak verification because the answers are often public or guessable. And even a verified user should not get MFA removed over the phone.

choices.label: None of these
choices.note: You refuse all three. Two teammates lean over with their own ideas.
choices.why: All three options act on the caller's word. When every option skips verification, the right call is to reject them and verify through a channel you control.

noneSuggestions.text: Hang up and call her back on the number in the company directory. If it's really her, she'll pick up.
noneSuggestions.short: Called back on the directory number

noneSuggestions.text: Keep MFA on and send her through the documented identity-verification process. No exceptions for rank.
Keep her talking and record the call. If she's fake, the recording might tell us who she is.
Stay on the line and pull her sign-in logs while she waits. The logs will tell us if it's her.

iris.hint: Whoever is on that line wants one thing: a door you leave open. A real CFO can survive five minutes of process.

echo.hint: Voices are easy to clone now. Don't trust the line. Trust a channel you chose yourself.

moritz.hint: The process exists so nobody has to judge a voice. If every option skips the process, none of them is right.

jayson.hint: Authority plus urgency. That's a pretext I'd use myself. Never act on an inbound call.

body.text: The real CFO answers on her directory number. She is in the board meeting and never called anyone. The help desk asks what to do now.
The real CFO calls from the boardroom: she never phoned the help desk. Her account is already being used. The help desk asks what to do now.

label.text: Revoke her sessions, restore MFA, log the incident and warn the help desk team about the caller
Log the attempt, warn the help desk team about the caller and share it with the security team

choices.note: The help desk gets a short warning with the caller's script. Two days later the same caller tries another agent, who hangs up.
choices.why: Failed attacks are still incidents. Recording and sharing them helps the team spot the next attempt, and the pattern may match other reports.

choices.label: Do nothing. No damage was done, or it can wait until Monday
choices.note: Nobody else hears about the call. The caller tries again next week with a better story.
choices.why: An unreported attempt teaches the attacker more than it teaches the defenders. Lessons learned only exist if someone writes them down.

choices.label: Post the caller's withheld number and voice recording on social media to warn others
choices.note: The post goes viral for the wrong reasons. Legal asks why internal incident details are public.
choices.why: Incident details are shared through agreed channels (security team, management, and if needed CERT or police), not posted publicly by an individual analyst.

choices.label: None of these
choices.note: You reject all three and wait for a better idea. Logging and warning the team was the right call here, so the extra hesitation costs you.
choices.why: "None of these" is only right when every option is wrong. Here one option followed good practice, so rejecting it costs extra points.

noneSuggestions.text: Write it up and brief the help desk.
Warn the help desk now; paperwork later.
Keep it to ourselves until we know more.

iris.hint: Nothing happened, so there is nothing to report. Paperwork only slows a good team down.

echo.hint: Write down the caller's exact words. Scripts repeat; that is how you recognise them next time.

moritz.hint: Post-incident activity is part of the process even when the attack failed. Record it and share it internally.

jayson.hint: Tell the help desk today. The same caller will try the next agent on shift.

endings.text: A convincing voice got past the help desk. In Master levels, the right answer is sometimes none of the options on the screen.
You verified before you trusted. That habit is what the Master levels test.

lessons: A familiar voice is not identity verification. Call back on a number you already have.
"None of these" is right only when every option on the screen is wrong.
In Master levels, a teammate's advice can be wrong. Know your team.
standards: NIST SP 800-61 (Computer Security Incident Handling Guide)
